explanations.answer: Who the crowds say He is
explanations.explanation: That's the very first question. Jesus asks, "Who do the crowds say I am?" (Luke 9:18). He starts with what everyone else is saying before He asks about the people right in front of Him. I think that's a smart way to ease into a big question.

Nice guess, friend, because people ask that one in the car every day. But this passage has no travel plans. Luke 9:18 says Jesus questioned them: "Who do the crowds say I am?" The question is about people, not directions.

explanations.answer: Which of them is the greatest
explanations.explanation: That topic does show up in Luke, but not here. An argument about which of them would be the greatest comes up later, in Luke 9:46. Here, Jesus asks them one thing first: "Who do the crowds say I am?" (Luke 9:18). The whole moment is about who He is.

Yep. The disciples answer, "Some say John the Baptist" (Luke 9:19). John was the man who preached baptism around the Jordan (Luke 3:3). So some people looked at Jesus and saw John. That's one theory out of several.

This one is actually true, friend. The disciples tell Jesus, "Some say John the Baptist" (Luke 9:19). John went around the Jordan preaching baptism (Luke 3:3). So some of the crowd really did think Jesus was John.

That's it. Peter answers, "The Christ of God" (Luke 9:20). The crowds were naming prophets, and Peter named something bigger. He said it plainly, no hedging. I've seen cookies hold a shape better than most people hold an answer under pressure, so that's a bold moment.
Close to what the crowds said, friend. Some of them said that "a prophet of old has arisen" (Luke 9:19). But Peter's answer is a different one. He says, "The Christ of God" (Luke 9:20).

It sounds right, but that word isn't in this answer. The crowds named John the Baptist, Elijah and a prophet of old (Luke 9:19). Then Peter answered, "The Christ of God" (Luke 9:20). So the missing word is Christ.

Here's the surprise. You'd expect Jesus to say, "Spread the word!" But Luke 9:21 says, "Jesus strictly warned them not to tell this to anyone." The text doesn't say why, so I won't guess. It says what He told them.

Right, and it's a surprise. Luke 9:21 says, "Jesus strictly warned them not to tell this to anyone." That's the opposite of go tell everyone. The text doesn't give a reason, so we leave it right there.

explanations.answer: The elders and chief priests and scribes
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus says the Son of Man "must be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes" (Luke 9:22). Those are three groups, and He names all of them. I think that's a hard thing to hear, and Jesus says it straight.

explanations.answer: The Roman governor and his soldiers
explanations.explanation: That's not who Jesus names in this passage. He says the Son of Man "must be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes" (Luke 9:22). Those are the three groups on His list. I'll stick to the list He gave.

explanations.answer: The tax collectors and the sinners
explanations.explanation: Not on this list, friend. In Luke 9:22, Jesus says He "must be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes." Those three are the ones He names. That's the whole list in this passage.

explanations.answer: He will be raised to life
explanations.explanation: That's the good part. Jesus says He "must be killed and on the third day be raised to life" (Luke 9:22). The hard news and the hopeful news come in the same sentence. Don't stop reading before the third day, baker.

explanations.answer: The temple will be torn down
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. In this passage, Jesus says the Son of Man "must be killed and on the third day be raised to life" (Luke 9:22). Nothing about a temple here. The third day is about Him being raised.
That's not what Jesus says here. He says the Son of Man "must be killed and on the third day be raised to life" (Luke 9:22). The third day belongs to Him being raised. That's the line to hold onto.
That's it. Jesus says, "he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me" (Luke 9:23). Notice the word daily. He doesn't say once, He says daily. No fine print, just plain words.

A staff is a good walking tool, but it's not in this verse. Jesus says, "he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me" (Luke 9:23). The thing to take up is a cross. And He says to do it daily.
Nope, no scrolls in this verse, friend. Jesus says, "he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me" (Luke 9:23). So the answer is the cross. And it's daily, not just once.
Jesus says the opposite. He says, "For whoever wants to save his life will lose it" (Luke 9:24). Trying to hold on tight ends in losing. It sounds backwards, and Jesus said it anyway.
Right. Jesus says, "For whoever wants to save his life will lose it" (Luke 9:24). It sounds backwards at first. But that's what the verse says, so we go with it.
Yes. Jesus says, "but whoever loses his life for My sake will save it" (Luke 9:24). Put the two halves together and it all fits. Losing it for His sake ends in saving it.

This one is true, friend. The second half of Luke 9:24 says, "but whoever loses his life for My sake will save it." The first half says saving your life loses it, and this half flips it around. Both halves are Jesus talking.

Yes. Jesus asks, "What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet lose or forfeit his very self?" (Luke 9:25). You could own everything and still lose the one thing that's you. I think that's a question worth sitting with.
A good name matters, but it's not what Jesus says. He asks about a man who gains the whole world and loses "his very self" (Luke 9:25). The thing at stake is himself. That's bigger than a name.
Land is a real thing to lose, but it's not in this verse. Jesus asks, "What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet lose or forfeit his very self?" (Luke 9:25). The answer is his very self.

explanations.answer: When He comes in His glory
explanations.explanation: That's what Jesus says. "If anyone is ashamed of Me and My words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when He comes in His glory" (Luke 9:26). This is one of the verses that keeps my ovens warm. It tells us He is coming in glory, but it doesn't tell us when.

That's not the moment Jesus names here. He says the Son of Man will be ashamed of that person "when He comes in His glory" (Luke 9:26). Jerusalem isn't mentioned in this passage. The time He gives is His coming in glory.

explanations.answer: When He goes up the mountain
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The time Jesus names is "when He comes in His glory" (Luke 9:26). No mountain is mentioned in this passage. He's talking about His coming.

explanations.answer: The Father and the holy angels
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says He comes "in His glory and in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels" (Luke 9:26). That's three glories in one sentence. Quite a list, baker.
They're not on this list. Moses, Israel's leader, isn't named in this verse. Jesus says He comes "in His glory and in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels" (Luke 9:26).
Not this time, friend. David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), isn't named in this verse. Jesus says He comes "in His glory and in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels" (Luke 9:26).

Yes. Jesus says, "some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God" (Luke 9:27). He opens with "I tell you truly," so I'm listening hard. And He's talking about people standing right there with Him.

Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (1 Kings 2:12), isn't in this verse. Jesus says, "some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God" (Luke 9:27). The thing they'll see is the kingdom of God.

That's not it, friend. Moses, Israel's leader, isn't mentioned in this verse. Jesus says, "some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God" (Luke 9:27). The answer is the kingdom of God.
